title: Video: Trump In Asia
text:
Video: Trump In Asia

Tom Miller

Gavekal Research

| 20 Nov 2026

The much-hyped Apec summit and Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting delivered little substance says Tom, but their diplomatic significance should not be overlooked. In this video interview, he discusses why the meetings themselves mattered, what they revealed about Trump’s continued influence abroad and how his more conciliatory approach signaled a renewed US commitment to Asia.

This transcript is auto generated.
Simon Pritchard: Welcome to this weekly Gavekal interview. I'm talking with Tom Miller today, and we are talking not about Anthropic, not about AI, but the round of summiteering that we've seen this week. First, the ASEAN meeting, then the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, and most particularly the meeting of the sort of big three, Russia, China, US leaders on the sidelines of that. And obviously, that was redolent of meetings past. So, Tom, when we look at what's happened this week, would you say we have had a new Yalta? And how significant would you say all of this has been?
Tom Miller: Right, before I get into the Yalta comparison, you know, I think it's worth saying what it was. I mean, usually when I do these talks after a big summit, Simon, I have to kind of make the case for why we should pay any attention at all. And, you know, because it is the case that these multilaterals, you know, rarely produce substantive agreements or move markets.
But in this case, of course, you know, this event really has received enormous attention, as you say, largely thanks to the historic trilateral meeting. It was unprecedented. It was the first meeting between the three leaders overseeing the world's largest nuclear arsenals. And of course, we have the political context of the Ukraine war, the Iran war, and also Trump's humiliation in the midterms. But was it a new Yalta?
You know, we had Zelensky warning just before the meeting that these three great powers are thinking of carving up the world and making decisions about smaller countries redolent of the meeting in Yalta in 1945. And at the meeting itself, both China and Russia called it groundbreaking. Trump said they're really making history. Of course, we don't know exactly what was said. It was a closed door meeting. But there were no concrete outcomes on Ukraine, on the Iran war, on nuclear disarmament. So, you know, it was not a lot of substance, if you like. And of course, it's worth thinking that the actual Yalta conference lasted a whole week. This was just 90 minutes.
So if you look at the major issues on Ukraine, Xi Jinping showed little interest, frankly, in being drawn into a discussion. It really isn't China's concern. And there was no attempt by Trump to dictate the terms of peace or design a new security architecture for Europe, any of those things that people are worried about in Europe. Iran was discussed, but it was omitted from the final declaration. You know, China, of course, doesn't want to get involved in a messy Middle Eastern war. And then on the nuclear issue, Xi Jinping said that nuclear weapons should be prohibited. But of course, China itself is actually building a stockpile faster than anyone else. The Pentagon projects that China's stockpile of nuclear warheads will exceed 1,000 by 2030. It's trying to catch up, of course, with the other two.
So I think what we saw was lots of political signalling and also, frankly, quite a lot of nonsense spoken. You know, they declared, so they announced a peace declaration, despite the fact that two of these countries are currently at war. Trump also hailed his very special relationship between the US and China, despite the fact that both are engaged in a historic rivalry. And I think, you know, talks of the birth of a new order, a new international order, were massively overdone.
What we're seeing really is more the undermining of the old one. So they made a commitment to reform the UN, though it's hard to see how anyone could possibly agree on how that would look. And they attacked the International Criminal Court, which tries to hold leaders, like these three leaders, accountable for what they do.
What it did do, I suppose, is cement the image of China again as a prime global player. Xi Jinping positioned himself in the middle, rather as Roosevelt did at Yalta in 1945. But of course, in reality, you know, China doesn't want the responsibility of running the world. So what I'd say is it was a very sort of important piece of political theatre, if you like, but with little substance below it.
And, you know, it really wasn't a market moving event. I think that's what's relevant for our clients. You know, they did announce an increase in the production supply of refined petroleum products. But if you look at the oil price yesterday, Brent actually ticked up very, very slight, very, very slightly. You know, Trump has already suspended most Russian related tariffs and new sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act. And U.S. Treasury has already announced a six month waiver of sanctions against the trade in Russian diesel. So this really made little difference.
If you look at the Trump's Xi Jinping bilateral, you know, that could have been actually a bigger market moving event. But again, you know, very little happened. There was no extension of the trade truce beyond January the 10th. We'll have to wait until the meeting in Miami next month. There was no breakthrough on rare earths, on tech exports. There are no announcements on tariffs or on Chinese purchases. So what we really saw was a massaging of Trump's ego. You know, that may help keep relations on track for the rest of his presidency.
We did see the formal establishment of the Board of Trade. They had their first meeting. You know, so there's a dedicated mechanism now for managing trade disputes that could be helpful. But in short, I think the absence of any big deals really means, in effect, it was no big deal at all.
Simon Pritchard: Well, you seem to be making a strong case, Tom, for us wrapping up this interview right now. As you said, no substance, no market moving news, but we're not going to do that. So looking at this, I mean, there must be reasons when we've had such three big powers, big leaders congregating why we do care about this.
Tom Miller: Sure, of course. So, I mean, diplomacy does matter. And this was diplomacy at the very highest level. And I suppose you could say it's a bit of a cliche now, but the meeting is the message.
So it did confer legitimacy and global status on Putin, who was clearly delighted by the meeting. You know, Trump was very publicly welcoming Putin back into the international fold. This was the second meeting the US president has had with Putin since the invasion of Ukraine. And I suppose we could conclude that Trump may now put further pressure on Ukraine and make more concessions to Russia.
It was also important, I think, because of the context at home in the US. Obviously, Trump has been weakened by the midterms. And the meeting was also taking place immediately after the Jensen Huang spy controversy. And yes, Trump may now be a lame duck president, but a lame duck president can still act abroad. That is an area in which actually Congress doesn't have that much power to act. And Trump, of course, now wants to secure his legacy. So, you know, sort of making grand gestures. And even making peace, if he could do that, whether it's in Ukraine or Iran, you know, that would be very, very helpful to securing that legacy.
And it's also an opportunity to discuss and shape, you know, great power relations. So I'm not sure Trump really is showing any sign of knowing what he wants to do in that area. And some of the subjects on the table do have high economic and commercial relevance. So we're talking about tariffs, chips, critical minerals, energy security, all of those issues.
And I think beyond the trilateral and the bilateral, you know, these are the meetings on the side of what was meant to be, you know, the APEC summit. And we mustn't forget APEC itself. And this is something which China particularly has always taken very, very seriously. I mean, it's worth noting, I think, that Xi Jinping sometimes skips the G20. He skips the UN General Assembly. He never skips APEC. I think that tells you something.
And, you know, we saw actually four formal multilateral summits this week. We saw the ASEAN meeting first. That's the meeting of the Southeast Asian nations. We saw the East Asia summit, which is ASEAN plus other powers in the region. And we saw the meeting of the quad leaders. And we saw plenty of other bilaterals on the side. So, for example, Xi Jinping also met the leaders of Canada, Mexico, Peru, Chile and Australia.
Simon Pritchard: Let's just jump into those. We've got a long list there. Let's look at the multilateral talks then. So, let's go with APEC first of all, as you said. Big Chinese priorities. So, did anything material come out of that meeting?
Tom Miller: Well, I mean, APEC is, to be quite frank with you, it's rarely very interesting. It's a useful platform for economic diplomacy. But it's not really there for making sort of big global decisions. It has more of a practical focus on trade facilitation, investment and economic cooperation, all those sorts of things. It has no binding powers. And it makes decisions by consensus.
But what it was, though, was an opportunity for Xi, again, to kind of call for freer trade and the open development of AIs. It's another chance to show that China is a responsible power and implicitly a more reliable partner than the U.S. It's very hard at this forum to secure, I think, meaningful support for trade integration amid ongoing U.S. protectionism. And China, of course, itself is also withholding some exports of rare earth permanent magnets. So, it's hardly the paragon of free trade that it likes to project.
What we did have was the so-called Shenzhen Outlook document, the sort of communique that was released at the end. And it calls for greater supply chain resilience and for the countries to address economic choke points. Of course, this is precisely, actually, what the U.S. is trying to sort of reduce, you know, it's trying to reduce dependence on China when it comes to rare earths and permanent magnets. And that's a fellow APEC member.
It also, the Outlook document also reaffirmed commitment to the long discussed but actually politically impossible idea of implementing a free trade area of the Asia Pacific. I don't see, you know, that is just, that's a pipe dream, something that China talks about, but it's not going to happen.
When it comes to substantive things, well, I think we can say that on the sidelines, China and Canada met. So, Xi Jinping met with Carney and they did extend tariff relief. And, you know, China-Canadian relations are now really back on track. Again, Xi Jinping today met Albanese, Australia. Something similar is happening there. Canada is working very hard to try to diversify trade away from the U.S. because of its own problems with the U.S. But I think overall, we can say that great power diplomacy, even though nothing much happened in substance, did overshadow APEC's traditional work on trade and economic integration.
Simon Pritchard: Right. Well, let's turn our attention, go a little bit smaller in terms of the number of nations involved. What about the ASEAN and the East Asia summits? What would Trump's attendance to those tell us about the U.S. policy in the region to start with?
Tom Miller: Yes. So, for summits themselves, not very much to say about them. So, I think what is interesting is Trump's attendance. So, this is the second year that Trump has attended the ASEAN meeting. That doesn't usually happen. He only attended one meeting in his first term and Biden skipped the summits in both 2023 and 2024. So, I think that shows some sustained attention to the region, despite fears that the U.S. is stepping away. That's something you always hear when you go to those countries. They worry that they want a U.S. presence, a strong U.S. presence, but they worry that the U.S. doesn't really care anymore.
So, I think the region is trying to gauge U.S. commitment, especially after last year's visit, where Trump was very, very bullying. You know, with lots of... He just slapped his tariffs on those countries and was demanding protection money, essentially. If you remember, demanding that Japan and South Korea invest massive amounts in the U.S. and basically, he was sort of unsettling all those relationships.
This shorter trip this time was much less coercive and nakedly transactional. It was more conciliatory, if you like. There was more of an emphasis on regional security and cooperation. He wasn't talking about tariffs. You know, there was talk behind the scenes on trade concessions, but it wasn't as sort of mafia-like, if you... It's one way, I think, of putting it. Of course, it doesn't mean that he's not transactional. You know, Thailand, for example, is close to closing a trade deal, which would eliminate tariffs on 99% of U.S. goods. And, you know, that is part of the deal. But he was certainly... He certainly projected a friendlier image.
I would say to come to meetings themselves, I think there were three important ones involving the U.S. So the first one was the U.S. ASEAN Special Summit, and that did produce a five-year cooperation package. So they were looking at maritime security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies, critical minerals and energy. And this is still very much the U.S. employing the stick and sort of, you know, sort of getting tough on China.
And I think here it's worth pointing out that Trump was arriving just after the U.S. crackdown, or the announcement of the crackdown on chip exports and renting compute in third countries. And so Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia were all targeted in this. You know, these countries want to be neutral digital hubs, but the U.S. is trying to force them to pick sides. It wants these third countries with data centres to police Chinese customers. And Prime Minister of Singapore, Lawrence Wong, said explicitly that Singapore will facilitate trade checks on chips, but it will not enforce U.S. export controls. So this kind of highlights the difficulty of balancing U.S. demands against these countries' sort of Chinese economic ties, which they don't want to break.
I think the other, the second important meeting was that between Trump and President Marcos of the Philippines. You know, under the previous president, the Philippines, the traditional treaty ally of the U.S. could have moved closer to China. It's really moved back into alignment with the U.S. And Trump reaffirmed U.S. defence commitments there. You know, Washington has approved $5 billion worth of fighter jets and arms sales over the last couple of years, although Manilla can't actually afford them.
And then I think the final thing to look at is the Quad Leaders Meeting, which has really not gained much attention because of all the other things going on. But it is important, you know, because I think a couple of years ago or last year, people wondered whether the Quad was dead. And this is the grouping of the U.S., India, Japan and Australia as a sort of quasi-security grouping. But with Trump's tariffs and with his attack, particularly on India, people thought he killed it off. The last leaders meeting in Delhi was actually cancelled because of this.
And this time, you know, I think the key was actually the meeting itself, the fact that it happened. But there was some substance. we're going to get some, there's a new maritime surveillance initiative and joint military exercises. They spoke about critical minerals. The details are very, very thin and also some cooperation on the AI supply chain. But once again, as with the trilateral, I think really the meeting is the message. And, you know, Trump's presence at the Quad and at the other meetings in Asia at least shows that the U.S. remains committed to Asian security. So that is one good thing to come out of this, out of this visit.
